+# Specification: `sort_list`
+
+## Overview
+
+`sort_list` takes a list of integers and returns a new list. The function is defined by the following postconditions; any implementation satisfying both conditions is correct.
+
+## Signature
+
+```python
+def sort_list(items: list[int]) -> list[int]
+```
+
+## Formal Specification
+
+Let `items` be the input list of integers and `result` be the returned value.
+
+**Postcondition 1 — Permutation.**
+`result` is a permutation of `items`. That is, there exists a bijective mapping `p : {0, ..., len(result) - 1} → {0, ..., len(items) - 1}` such that for all indices `i`, `result[i] == items[p(i)]`. Equivalently, every value occurring `n` times in `items` occurs exactly `n` times in `result`, and the two lists have equal length:
+
+    len(result) == len(items)
+    ∀ v ∈ ℤ : count(result, v) == count(items, v)
+
+**Postcondition 2 — Sortedness.**
+`result` is sorted in non-decreasing order. That is, for all valid indices `i` and `j`, if `i < j` then `result[i] <= result[j]`. Adjacent-pair form (equivalent):
+
+    ∀ i ∈ {0, ..., len(result) - 2} : result[i] <= result[i + 1]
+
+## Notes
+
+- The input list is not mutated: `items` is unchanged after the call, and `result` is a distinct list object.
+- Postcondition 1 and Postcondition 2 together uniquely determine the output: there is exactly one list satisfying both, so `sort_list` is deterministic.
+- The empty list sorts to the empty list; both postconditions hold vacuously.
